article_text:
UPDATED with Once Upon A Time In Harlem , Musk , more : Netflix ‘s Spanish drama La Bola Negra debuted to $277.5k on four screens – these numbers coming directly from the giant streamer Sunday in its first ever official box office grosses.

The TIFF audience award-winner saw $108.3k Friday and $84.6k on Saturday leading into a strong three-day per screen average of $69.4k for the company’s inaugural report.

The film, based on an unfinished play of the same name by Federico García Lorca, launched at the Paris Theater and Angelika in New York, and AMC Century City and Burbank in LA. Netflix is giving the festival favorite a 45-day theatrical window in a new era of box office reporting overseen by global theatrical distribution head Spencer Klein. It will expand in NY/LA and add major markets over the next few weeks ahead of a wider break 11/6.

Related Stories

'Nobody Wants This' Creator Erin Foster Has "More Story To Tell" With A Season 4, But Isn't Getting "Too Attached"

Quentin Tarantino Wraps His AFI Fest Q&A By Showing Crowd First 17 Minutes Of 'Cliff Booth'

House records, as per Netflix, reflect the highest opening gross for a non-English language film at the Angelika, The Paris and AMC Century City (excluding dubbed anime) and, more broadly, the second-highest per-screen average for a non-English language film of all time. And the highest per-screen average ever for a Spanish film.

Watch on Deadline

Buzz for the film began at its Cannes world premiere where helmers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi shared Best Director for the R-rated, era-spanning story that went on to beguile the festival circuit. Spain’s Oscar entry for Best International Feature follows the interconnected lives of three gay men.

Netflix gave the film a full theatrical marketing campaign including out-of-home, social, standees, trailers and community screenings, along with bespoke elements. A poetry salon hosted by John Cameron Mitchell and modeled on Lorca’s secret 1930s intellectual gatherings, brought filmmakers and cast together to honor Lorca’s lasting influence on queer art and culture ahead of the NYC premiere last Thursday at NewFest. Marketing will be key for and upcoming titles as the company seeks to draw moviegoers into seats.

The streamer release Guitarricadelafuente’s single from the film, ‘La Nieve,’ (The Snow) on Sept. 18. The musician made his acting debut in the film, which also stars Milo Quifes and Carlos González., with Glenn Close and Penélope Cruz.

Reactions from in-theater audience exit surveys were strong with 96% rating La Bola Negra Excellent or Very Good (80% Excellent), and 87% giving it a Definite Recommend. The film skewed male (66%) and young, with 51% under 35 and 25 to 34 year-olds the largest age group at 39%.

It’s Rotten Tomatoes Certified Fresh with critics at 87%.

Upcoming Netflix releases set for wider theatrical release and significant windows include The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth by David Fincher; Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew ; animated feature Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory : by Taika Waititi; The Mosquito Bowl by Peter Berg and Danny Boyle’s Ink .

Neon had a notable weekend as Once Upon A Time In Harlem eyes $68.3k on two NYC screens opening weekend, a $34k per screen average. Presales and lively walk-up business saw sold-out shows and filmmaker Q&As for this unique project that was 50 years in the making.

Directed by David Greaves, it was started by his father, the late William Greaves, who captured on film a 1972 cocktail party he hosted at Duke Ellington’s house with living luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. For four hours, this extraordinary group, many of whom had not seen each other in 50 years, reminisced, critiqued, argued, laughed and drank while wrestling with their place in a rapidly shifting cultural landscape.

The doc world premiered at Sundance and screened at Cannes Directors’ Fortnight, Telluride, Toronto and New York Film Festival, where it won the Library of Congress Lavine/Ken Burns Prize for Film. At 100% RT Certified Fresh, the doc is Film Forum’s highest opening weekend for any picture this year. Neon adds LA next week with filmmaker Q&As then rolls out regionally with its widest footprint in early- mid November.

The distributor’s Cannes Palme d’Or winner Fjord delivered $124.5k in on 13 screens (up from 4) in a limited week two expansion. Moves to 100 runs next week, then to 500 nationally. A strong 91% from RT reviewers, with an 89% audience score.

Bleecker Street’s Alex Gibney doc Musk grossed an estimated $307k in a nationwide expansion across 472 screens for a cume of $395k. RT certified fresh at 97% but the distributor called out repeated issues with major social media platforms. That includes an inability to advertise on giant X, which is owned by Musk, and, this weekend, seeing TikTok, the leading platform for its core audience, permanently suspend the film’s ad account at a critical juncture with the film expanding.

Add to that a nearly four-hour runtime that limits shows, and the turnout from markets all over the country shows an audience is still finding the film. LA, New York and the San Francisco Bay Area are the top markets this weekend, with the Bay Area posting the strongest per-screen average in the country. Specialty and arthouse theaters are playing an outsized role, led by the Angelika in New York, with business spread broadly beyond the two coasts’ largest cities.

Musk also faced off with A24’s insanely buzzy doc You Can See Everything , which had extraordinary weekend gross of $15 million at just 855 locations — one of the largest openings ever for any film under 1,000 screens. Made in secret over three years, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s portrait of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the days before she reported to prison to start a ten-year term for fraud made its surprise world premiere at Telluride and has since become a cultural phenomenon.

NAZA , by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor expanded to 105 engagements (from 85) in week three for an estimated three-day gross of $178k and a $886k cume.

Indian Tamil language action-comedy Jailer 2 from Schloka Entertainment, was no. 9 at the box office with $3.2 million on 401 screens for a cume of $5.3 million. Directed by Nelson Dilipkumar. And Telugu romantic action comedy Ranabaali from Prathyangira Cinemas opened to $719k from 375 theaters. Directed by Rahul Sankrityan. Both as per Rentrak.

Spider horror Crawler s from Roadside Attractions opened to $468k at 1,037 theaters.

EVENT : The Met: Live in HD transmission of Verdi’s Macbeth, the second live performance of the 20th anniversary season of opera on the big screen, grossed $710k ion 800 screens. Conducted by Yannick Nézet-Séguin, the Met’s Jeanette Lerman-Neubauer Music Director, and starring soprano Lise Davidsen and baritone Quinn Kelsey, it will have encore screenings in select cinemas in the U.S. on Oct. 21 and Canada Nov. 21.

article_text:
Five days after Bela Bajaria was fired as Netflix ‘s Chief Content Officer and replaced by Peter Rice , Ted Sarandos had nothing but kind words for his former loyal lieutenant, kinda.

“Bela had an incredible decade-long run here,” the amped up co-CEO said during Netflix’s Q3 earnings call Tuesday, praising the decade-long employee “for all of her incredible contributions.”

Related Stories

Netflix Stock Falls Despite Solid Q3 Results On Lowered Q4 Revenue And Advertising Guidance

Peter Rice Will Blend “Art And Commerce” In Heading Content For Netflix, Ted Sarandos Says

Echoing a lot of the language he used in the October 15 internal memo announcing Bajaria’s axing, Sarandos today added: “She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local for local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

Watch on Deadline

“So, I just want to take that moment to to thank Bella,” Sarandos concluded before launching a soliloquy of sorts on how “thrilled” he is on Rice joining Netflix as the new CCO.

“I know we can do better,” Sarandos said, “we see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level.”

Bajaria was widely thought to be safe from the chopping block as Sarandos and Peters cut 1,000 jobs last week , including top-tier execs like VP Film Doug Belgrad . That assumption of Bajaria’s staying power, encouraged by internal nods and winks, was proved wrong 24 hours later with the news that she was out. Film boss Dan Lin was already on thin ice himself and that ice cracked for the Lego producer on Monday . No replacement for Lin has been announced, with the expectation Rice (aka Sarandos) will be naming someone soon-ish.

On an afternoon that saw Netflix stock slide more than 5% in after-hours trading even with solid Q3 results , Sarandos and co-CEO Greg Peters were “totally focused” as always. After a year that has seen the stock down 40%, the CEOs were focused on pitching the upcoming slate of originals, “core entertainment value,” engagement, partnerships like France’s TFI, live sports. The duo also appeared hyper-focused on ex-Disney exec Rice riding in on a corporate white horse next week to help clean up the joint. To that, for all the praise of Bajaria, there was much said about Rice and his relationships with talent. Nothing was uttered on today’s call in the specific realm of talent relationships about former CCO Bajaria.

Unlike that October 15 memo on Bajaria’s exit, Sarandos today also did not mention any of the names of the big titles like Squid Game and the upcoming The Adventures of Cliff Booth (though both Sarandos and Peters couldn’t seem to say the name “Tarantino” enough), the ex-CCO brought to the platform.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "致力于家庭照片归档的慈善机构 La Conserverie 正在南锡的普瓦雷尔画廊（Poirel Gallery）举办“Présent”展览。展期将持续至 11 月 21 日，这是面向所有人公开征集作品的成果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有些照片在我们的心中占据着特殊的位置。夹在钱包折缝里的一张挚爱之人的照片、书桌上装在相框里的儿童肖像，或是挂在客厅墙壁上的全家福。在南锡普瓦雷尔画廊展出的“Présent”展览，正是探讨了这种将我们与这一媒介紧密相连的极其特殊且私密的纽带。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展出的每一张照片都来自于展览主办方——La Conserverie 协会所发起的征集活动中的捐赠。数十位个人打开了他们的抽屉和个人相册，才让这场展览得以实现。这是对跨越多个不同时代的本土纪实摄影的一致美妙致敬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现场共展出了三个系列。“De l’air”汇集了一系列照片，其中所有拍摄对象都有一个共同特征，即他们的头发都被风吹乱了。许多照片拍摄于海边或河畔。 amused 的表情，也有烦躁的迹象：这些陌生人往往展现出相似的面部表情和反应。有些照片的装裱方式更为随性，而另一些则更为专业。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览还探讨了其他私密主题：参观者可以发现从陌生人钱包里找到的照片。妻子、孩子、祖父母：有些人甚至把他们的家庭相册随身揣在口袋里！展览的最后一部分玩味了“画中画”（mise en abîme）的概念。参与者被要求提交画面中包含其他照片的照片。参观者凑近照片，去寻找这些画中之画。此外，La Conserverie 正在继续其征集活动，并邀请任何希望以该主题发送个人影像的人与他们取得联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作品征集将持续至 2027 年 3 月 31 日，并将最终以一场展览以及一本摄影集的出版告终。您可以自行扫描照片（最低 1,200 dpi，未经编辑，JPEG 格式，并按“名-姓”格式命名），然后连同签署好的授权书一起发送。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "提交照片方式：邮寄：La Conserverie c/o Image’est – Pôle Image Manufacture, 9 rue Michel Ney, 54 000 Nancy。电子邮箱：[email protected]", "links": [{"text": "[email protected]", "url": "https://loeildelaphotographie.com/en/in-nancy-family-photographs-invests-poirel-gallery/cetaitoucetaitquand@free.fr"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Présent”展览：2026 年 9 月 24 日星期四至 2026 年 11 月 21 日，南锡维克托·普瓦雷尔街 3 号普瓦雷尔画廊（Galerie Poirel）。免费入场。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
The charity La Conserverie, which specialises in archiving family photographs, is organising the exhibition ‘Présent’ at the Poirel Gallery in Nancy. On display until 21 November, it is the result of a call for submissions open to everyone.

There are photographs that hold a special place in our hearts. A photo of a loved one tucked away in the folds of a wallet, a framed portrait of a child on a desk, or a family photo hanging on the living room wall. The ‘Présent’ exhibition, on display at the Poirel Gallery in Nancy, explores this very special and intimate bond that unites us with this medium.

Each of the photographs on display comes from donations, following a call for submissions organised by the association La Conserverie, the exhibition’s organiser. Dozens of individuals have opened up their drawers and personal albums to make this exhibition possible. It is a beautiful tribute to vernacular photography spanning a wide range of eras.

Three series are on display. ‘De l’air’ brings together a series of photographs in which the subjects all share the common feature of having their hair ruffled by the wind. Many were taken by the sea or a river. Amused expressions, but also signs of irritation: these strangers often display the same facial expressions and reactions. Some photos are framed in a more casual manner, whilst others are more professional.

The exhibition explores other intimate themes: visitors can discover the photos found in the wallets of strangers. A wife, children, grandparents: some people even carry their family albums in their pockets! The final section of the exhibition plays with the concept of ‘mise en abîme’. Participants were asked to submit photographs in which other photographs appeared within the frame. Visitors lean in to the photos to spot these images within images. Furthermore, La Conserverie is continuing its call for submissions and invites anyone wishing to send in personal images on this theme to get in touch.

The call for submissions is open until March 31st 2027 and will culminate in an exhibition and the publication of a book of photographs. You can scan the photographs yourself (minimum 1,200 dpi, unedited, in JPEG format, and name them using the format ‘first name-SURNAME’) and then send them along with a signed authorisation form.

Submitting photographs: By post: La Conserverie c/o Image’est – Pôle Image Manufacture, 9 rue Michel Ney, 54 000 Nancy. By email: [email protected]

‘Présent’ exhibition: From Thursday 24 September 2026 to 21 November 2026 Galerie Poirel, 3 rue Victor Poirel, Nancy. Free admission.

article_text:
會員評論

香港電影評論學會季刊 《HKinema》第七十期 同步出版 第七十期專題： 暴烈與流動： 動作電影的跨文化交鋒 今年，當谷垣健治執導的《火遮眼》上映並引發熱烈討論時，鏡頭前呈現的是多元面孔與異國場景，而在鏡頭背後，推動整場演出與技術核心的依然是一群香港電影人。正如已故電影學者大衛博維爾（David Bordwell）所觀察，不同地區的電影工業從來不是各自獨立的孤島，而是在歷史發展中互相影響、彼此借鏡。在這其中，「動作電影」往往是跨文化交流最直接、也最快見效的領域。

本期專題正是以此為起點展開多維度的審視。有宏觀脈絡與跨國對話：鄭政恆在〈殺破圍城火遮眼〉中，探討近十年香港電影工業逐漸萎縮下，動作電影究竟怎樣掙扎求存；美國影評人Jonah Jeng長期關注亞洲動作，重尋泰國與香港動作電影之間血脈相連的影響。亦有兩篇專訪：鏡頭轉向幕後實踐現場，了解為《火遮眼》擔任動作指導的園村健介，如何在跨國合作與動作真實感中建立風格；曾肇弘則訪問香港少見的女動作特技演員黃瑞琦，將目光投向陽剛氣極濃的特技生態，細數女性從業者的掙扎與突破。配合兩篇扉頁承傳與梳理動作電影的底蘊，以及另一篇關於「動作電影的跨文化」的文章，共同追問動作語彙在全球流散中的蛻變。 線上閲讀： https://bit.ly/4rExJjO 實體版可於以下地點 免費 索取： https://bit.ly/4ykwlFC 郵寄服務： https://bit.ly/3V6QRLt 第七十期目錄 前言 殺破圍城火遮眼：近十年香港動作電影觀察／鄭政恆 衝擊因子：當代泰國動作電影的香港脈絡／Jonah Jeng 打破成規，失序中拏攫真實：專訪《火遮眼》動作指導園村健介／何阿嵐 一招一式——動作特技基本功／李東阳 從陽剛中突圍——專訪動作特技演員黃瑞琦／曾肇弘、李東阳 Hip Hop「溝」邵氏武俠？——談動作片的跨國文化互動／ 何阿嵐

article_text:
Priyanka Chopra Jonas and Tony-winning activist-playwright V, formerly known as Eve Ensler , have signed on as executive producers of Pranav Bhasin’s Oscar-qualified Indian short “ We Were Here .” They join Andrew Scott as the film gears up for awards season.

The New Yorker has acquired the short and will premiere it on the magazine’s YouTube channels.

“We Were Here” has screened at more than 80 festivals and collected over 20 awards. It launched at the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival, taking the Canal+ Prize. At SXSW, it won the audience award for best narrative short along with the Redbreast Unhidden Award. Palm Springs International ShortFest named it best live-action short under 15 minutes and best comedy short, and that win made the film eligible for Academy Award consideration.

Related Stories

Omar Sy on Taking Creative Control of Netflix's 'Lupin' and Why 'Black Dumas' Will Spark Political Debate in France

Bhasin wrote and directed the mockumentary, set in a small Indian town. Three retirees, certain that machines are stealing human jobs, mount a protest by posing as household appliances. Their campaign is thrown off course when one of their children goes to work for an artificial intelligence company.

Satish Kashyap, Devendra Dodke and Arindol Bagchi star as Mr. Bagchi, Mr. Pimple and Mr. Ganguli. The cast also includes Shubham Kujur, Kalpana Gagdekar and Yash Gonsai. Gonsai produced through Sunshine Pictures alongside Dheer Momaya and Dar Gai. Aarti Lohia and SPLF Media present the film.

“This film offers a refreshing, witty take on a subject that feels very timely. I jumped at the opportunity to come on board as an executive producer to amplify this creative team and ensure their brilliant, original vision gets the spotlight it deserves,” said Chopra Jonas.

The executive producer roster also includes Peter S. Kim and Nalini Sharma of Basement Video, Neha Kaul, Megha Kadakia, Priya Giri Desai and Shruti Ganguly of Prism Entertainment, Shivani Pandya Malhotra, Film Companion Studios, Anjula Acharia and Pan Nalin. Devaiah Bopanna, Earlyman Film, Rahul Bharti, Supavitra Babul and Vaibhav Bundhoo are co-producers.

Bhasin, who hails from Mumbai, was directing films by the age of 13 and had made his first series, for TVF, by 17. At the Mumbai film festival, his short “Wolf of Chawl Street” took the Silver Dimensions prize in 2017, and “New Year’s Eve” was named best short a year later. His other work includes “Taylor’s Version” and “Screaming on the Fly.” His films have premiered at SXSW and on Mubi, Short of the Week and Vimeo Staff Picks. He is an alumnus of Vanishing Angle’s Short-to-Feature Lab (2020) and the Zurich Film Festival Academy (2022).

“‘We Were Here’ started as a small, silly idea about three uncles trying to stop the spread of AI, and somewhere along the way, I fell in love with them, their friendships, and their stubborn resilience. In India, reality is often stranger than anything you could write, and the mockumentary format let me keep the film rooted in real people and real places, while exploring just how absurd things can get,” said Bhasin. “Now that the film is Oscar-qualified, I’m still figuring out how to process it. I made it the way I make everything. I followed an idea that felt wild to me, all the way to the end. I was never sure it would make sense to anyone outside my head. As a young filmmaker, I find it pretty surreal to have a tribe of highly accomplished and committed EPs, including Andrew Scott, Priyanka Chopra Jonas, and V. We’re all really excited to find creative ways to get this film to wider audiences.”

Gonsai was an executive producer on Nalin’s “Last Film Show,” which made the international feature shortlist at the 95th Academy Awards. He more recently teamed with Dharma Productions on Neeraj Ghaywan’s Cannes-debuting “Homebound,” which was shortlisted at the 98th Academy Awards.

article_text:
No one familiar with the oeuvre of Peter Berg — the action merchant behind the Afghanistan war drama “Lone Survivor” and the improbably pumped-up boardgame adaptation “Battleship” — should approach “ The Mosquito Bowl ” expecting great restraint or good taste. Ostensibly, Berg’s Netflix -backed combat epic is fighting the same fight as Terrence Malick’s “The Thin Red Line,” likewise charting the physical and psychological torment of American soldiers in Guadalcanal during the Pacific Theater of the Second World War. But they are two very different history lessons. There’s not a hint of Malick’s poetic anti-war melancholy in Berg’s brawny, cacophonous Semper Fi salute to American military brotherhood, which certainly doesn’t stray from standard war-is-hell sentiment — rarely, in fact, has war been depicted as more loudly ruinous — but positively revels in onscreen carnage, as if to underline the mettle of its Marine heroes.

Not that said mettle is in any danger of going unnoticed. For the four men at the pretty hollow center of “The Mosquito Bowl” aren’t just soldiers but sportsmen — stars of the college football circuit who bring their strength and smarts from the field to the battlefield. And if that comparison sounds glib to you, then buckle up, because the film has plenty more: “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in the history of football,” says one character, a sentiment that sounds sort of rousing without making much sense. That goes for much of the script by Berg and Mark L. Smith, which is drawn from a popular 2022 historical novel by Buzz Bissinger — the journalist whose 1990 bestseller “Friday Night Lights” became the basis of Berg’s sturdy 2004 football drama and the more popular TV series spun off from it.

Berg and Bissinger are cousins; the screen adaptation of “The Mosquito Bowl” was likely a fait accompli all along. Yet while the book’s ennobling mixture of Greatest Generation portraiture and brutal evocation of the rigors of combat is perfectly tailored to the filmmaker’s interests, it also hands the screenwriters a bit of a structural red herring. The title refers to a football game that the principals were tasked with organizing on Guadalcanal; it was played on Christmas Eve 1944 between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division, and featured a wealth of drafted football talents who had set aside their sporting careers to serve their country. Outwardly, the book and film both seek to imbue this event with the significance of the famed Christmas truce soccer matches between British and German forces in the no-man’s-land of the First World War.

When push comes to shove, however, the game simply isn’t all that consequential. It’s skipped over surprisingly swiftly on the page, and despite much anticipatory buildup, the film, too, struggles to make a climactic set-piece of an event that has considerably less visceral impact than the various juddering, blood-on-the-lens battle scenes on either side of it. Nor does it work as a human interlude, because the human dimension of “The Mosquito Bowl” is so flimsy. Its four principals are colorless, interchangeable alpha males, uniformly stout of build and square of jaw; they’re granted mildly differing character attributes by the script, but even as the closing credits roll, you’d be hard pressed to remember who was who.

John McLaughry ( Nicholas Galitzine ), a graduate (and future football coach) of Brown University, is given the leading perspective — which is to say he occupies the framing scenes that have him visiting a college football field years after the war with a stoic, misty gaze, and reflecting vaguely on all that has been won and lost. We rewind to 1941, when the earnest young man’s budding future with the New York Giants is put on ice by a surge of patriotic duty in the wake of Pearl Harbor; the same goes for jocular Purdue grad Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, appropriating his father Jack’s rakish perma-grin), soulfully withdrawn Wisconsin Badgers star Dave Schreiner (stage star Tom Francis, a Tony nominee for “Sunset Blvd.”), and fellow Wisconsin grad Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), whose personality lands somewhere between those last two — the writers having run out of all-American archetypes quite early on.

Historical dates are lightly fudged to give the four men a shared soldierly narrative, and so they collectively endure the grueling trials of Parris Island basic training, horrible but familiar from many a military drama, before shipping out to the Pacific, where the shattering, deafening mayhem that awaits them is horrible but familiar from many a war movie. Knowing that he has nothing new to show us, Berg’s solution is to show us ever more of the same, ladling on the frank images of death and devastating injury with relentless rat-a-tat-tat sound design to the point that the film does attain a blunt sensory force.

The aesthetic, with DP Jacques Jouffret’s aggressively desaturated palette and nauseous POV shooting coupled with antsy, abrasive editing, is ripped from “Saving Private Ryan,” but cranked up to video game levels, with a grinding, guitar-heavy score by post-rock band Explosions in the Sky; the film’s technical proficiency so overwhelms its slender character-building that it begins to feel almost heartless.

The actors, all talented, are given no scope to be any more than capable. There’s scant room for inner life here, nor for reflection on anything more specific than war’s general cruelty — though, needless to say, the enemy gets even shorter shrift. There’s a jingoistic undertow to “The Mosquito Bowl,” with its flag-waving celebration of football and Marine fortitude, that sits queasily with decontextualized shots of Japanese soldiers committing ritual seppuku or being summarily executed by American captors, or the main characters’ repeated gung-ho statements about “killing the Japanese.” The film strains to say something about the morally corrupting effects of warfare, but doesn’t challenge its heroic leads on the racist invective they parrot, or circle back to any regret they may feel deeper into their service. Trivial and shoehorned in as it seems, when the titular football game rolls along, you can practically feel the film’s sigh of relief: at last, a blessed few minutes of macho combat without consequences — or politics.

article_text:
Sakhya Byamba’s “ Zogsool ” was the biggest winner at the Busan International Film Festival ’s Vision Awards on Wednesday, taking home four prizes.

The film won both the Netpac Award and the Fipresci Award, along with the Vision of Jiseok Award. It also shared the Hylife Vision Award with Sailesh Rathnakumar’s “ Selvi ,” which separately picked up the Taipei Film Commission Award.

Related Stories

'Amanda the Adventurer' Video Game Movie Adaptation in the Works From Blumhouse, MatPat and Epic Pictures

Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,' Teases Joining 'True Detective'

Among Korean titles, Jeong Jihye’s “ Full Moon ” won three prizes: the CGV Award, the K-Movie Award and the Songwon Vision Audience Award – Korea. Park Songyeol’s “Beyond Love’s Horizon” won the KBS Independent Film Award and the Critic b Award, and Won Hyangra received one of two Actor of the Year honors for her work in the film. Kang Seung-ho took the other for “Cosmic Trace.”

Oh Sehyeon’s “Baler” won twice, with the Jeong-in Award and the Citizen Critics’ Award. Kim Si-jin’s “The Flower” received the DGK Plus M Award.

The BIFF Mecenat Award in the Asian category went to Yang Bo’s “Agaar,” and Yi Seungjun’s “Can I Talk to You?” won the Korean award. Choi Se-dam’s “A Woman Dancing on the Waves” got a special mention.

Soroush Shahpouri’s “Fatima” won the Asian Sonje Award, and Yun Taerang’s “Toe’s” won the Korean one. Jung Jaeseo’s “The Boy Who Fell to Earth” was singled out with a special mention.

Kumamoto Ryohei’s “After the Song” won the Face of the Future Award, and Arvin Belarmino’s “Ria” won The Heart of Eurasia Award. “There Will Be Snow,” from Chen Jianying, received the Bishkek International Film Festival-Central Asia Cinema Award. Darkhan Tulegenov’s “The Cord” took the International Film Festival of India – Vision Asia Award.

Audiences picked Shashank Walia’s “Birds in the Dark” for the Songwon Vision Audience Award – Asia. Im Yeonjeong’s “Recovery” won the Documentary Audience Award, and “La Bola Negra,” directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, won the Flash Forward Audience Award. Janay Boulos and Abd Alkader Habak’s “Birds of War” won the Busan Cinephile Award.

The 31st edition of the festival opened Oct. 6 and will close Oct. 15. Its industry arm, the Asian Contents & Film Market, ran from Oct. 10 to Oct. 13.

article_text:
La muerte de RJ Mitte , reconocido mundialmente por interpretar a Walter White Jr. en Breaking Bad , conmocionó a Hollywood y especialmente a quienes compartieron con él los años de rodaje de la exitosa serie.

El actor falleció el lunes 12 de octubre a los 34 años, según confirmó su representante. Entre las numerosas despedidas, una de las más emotivas fue la de Bryan Cranston , quien interpretó a su padre en la ficción y mantuvo una relación cercana con él incluso después del final de la producción.

A través de su cuenta de Instagram, Cranston publicó una extensa carta en la que recordó sus primeros encuentros con Mitte, su crecimiento profesional y el vínculo que construyeron durante más de una década.

La emotiva despedida de Bryan Cranston

Cranston comenzó su mensaje expresando el profundo dolor que le provocó la noticia. El actor recordó que conoció a Mitte cuando tenía apenas 14 años, después de que fuera seleccionado para interpretar a Walter White Jr., el hijo adolescente de Walter y Skyler White.

Desde el comienzo, destacó su entusiasmo por la actuación y la determinación con la que enfrentaba las exigencias de una producción televisiva de semejante magnitud. También recordó cómo él y Anna Gunn, quien interpretaba a Skyler, intentaban aconsejarlo durante los rodajes, aunque el joven actor, como cualquier adolescente, no siempre seguía sus recomendaciones.

Se reveló la causa de muerte de RJ Mitte, actor de Breaking Bad

Bryan Cranston habló sobre su retiro de la actuación

Con el paso de las temporadas, Cranston fue testigo de su transformación en un intérprete cada vez más experimentado.

El encuentro que nunca llegó a concretarse

Uno de los momentos más conmovedores de la publicación llegó cuando Cranston reveló que ambos habían intercambiado mensajes apenas unas semanas antes de la muerte de Mitte. Los actores estaban intentando organizar un almuerzo para reencontrarse, pero ese encuentro nunca llegó a concretarse.

Cranston se preguntó si aquella reunión podría haber cambiado algo, aunque reconoció que nunca tendrá una respuesta. El actor cerró su despedida con un:

“Te voy a extrañar, hijo”.

Sus palabras reflejan un vínculo que trascendió la pantalla y continuó mucho después de que Breaking Bad emitiera su último episodio en 2013.

¿Quién era RJ Mitte?

Nacido el 21 de agosto de 1992, Roy Frank Mitte III , conocido artísticamente como RJ Mitte, alcanzó la fama internacional gracias a su interpretación de Walter White Jr., también llamado Flynn, en Breaking Bad .

El personaje era el hijo de Walter White, interpretado por Cranston, y Skyler White, interpretada por Anna Gunn.

Mitte participó en las cinco temporadas de la serie creada por Vince Gilligan, que se emitió entre 2008 y 2013 y se convirtió en una de las producciones más aclamadas de la historia de la televisión.

Al igual que su personaje, Mitte tenía parálisis cerebral, una condición que lo llevó a involucrarse activamente en la defensa de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad.

Después del final de Breaking Bad , continuó trabajando en cine y televisión y participó en producciones como Switched at Birth , Triumph y Standing Up for Sunny .

Además, desarrolló una importante actividad como defensor de la inclusión y la representación de las personas con discapacidad dentro de la industria audiovisual.

La despedida del elenco de Breaking Bad

Cranston no fue el único integrante de la serie que expresó su tristeza. Aaron Paul , quien interpretó a Jesse Pinkman, y Dean Norris , recordado por su papel de Hank Schrader, también compartieron mensajes en memoria de su compañero.

La muerte de Mitte generó numerosas reacciones entre los seguidores de Breaking Bad , una serie que, a más de una década de su final, continúa ocupando un lugar fundamental en la cultura popular.

Según confirmó su representante, el actor murió por suicidio. En su despedida, Cranston también hizo un llamado a quienes atraviesan situaciones de sufrimiento emocional para que busquen acompañamiento y ayuda profesional.

Más allá de su recordado papel como Walter White Jr., RJ Mitte deja un legado vinculado a la actuación, la inclusión y la representación de las personas con discapacidad .

Y para Bryan Cranston, además de un compañero de trabajo, siempre será aquel adolescente al que vio crecer durante cinco temporadas y al que todavía recordaba como su hijo.

article_text:
We re-publish this article to commemorate the life and work of artist Dinh Q. Lê (Lê Quang Đỉnh) who has left us too soon. It is part of ‘An Assignment on Memory’, a series of essays by the young writer Carmen Cortizas Fontan, first launched in December 2022. This project was supported by the Nguyen Art Foundation and made possible with support from the artist Nguyen Van Cuong. The article is translated by Nguyen Thanh Tam.

In the temples of Angkor Wat, rows upon rows of headless Buddha statues sit on old stone. The bodies have been chipped with time, and scratches of violence can be seen around the necks. The heads have been taken to different cities around the world. In their new homes, they are often placed on a white pedestal, with a plexiglass on top and called pieces of art.

Although both the ‘bodied’ and the ‘disembodied’ share the same painful history, their decades of separation have caused them to become independent of each other. This story directly speaks to the violent looting of South East Asian heritage in the process of colonization, but to artist Dinh Q. Lê, it also embodies a portrait of himself, and of others who have experienced the dichotomy of being a refugee.

Having grown up with America’s portrayal of Vietnam since he arrived there at the age of ten, Dinh is especially aware of the Western-centric narratives that continuously dominate history. His work is an attempt to give unheard stories an opportunity to integrate and infiltrate into mainstream historical discourse, thus contributing to a more complex understanding of Vietnamese identity – beyond that of an extra in American war movies.

Since his youth, Dinh has been deeply interested in the role of the photographer, and the influence that photographs can have in different socio-political contexts. While attending the New York School of Visual Arts, he began to research the photographic narrative produced by Vietnamese photojournalists on the Viet Minh side 1 – whose images weren’t put on the front pages of Life Magazine or the New York Times. With a research grant, Dinh returned to Vietnam in 1992, where in Hanoi, he was able to find a group of photojournalists that let him view their mostly unseen photographs. Although the photographs were laid on the table for him, he was not permitted to take any pictures or use them for his own purposes, due to the fear that it could be used against the photographers in some way.

Amongst other experiences Dinh encountered during his first weeks in Vietnam, this incident proved to him the distrust people had towards Viet Kieus 2 . This feeling of being a foreigner in his place of birth – disoriented and unaware, ironically could be likened to his experience arriving in the United States. Thus, Dinh decided to begin his journey of “re-learning how to be Vietnamese”, which eventually laid the seed for his permanent stay in Vietnam.

In the early 1990s, although the Vietnam War had ended, its legacy continued through the presence of Agent Orange, as seen in people with deformities on the streets of Saigon. The government and society at large, however, treated it as a taboo subject.

Thinking about how such a horrific issue could be translated into the context of a post-Doi Moi society eagerly trying to turn the page of war, for his 1998 series Damaged Gene , Dinh approached the owner of a children’s clothing kiosk in a popular shopping mall in downtown District 1 and offered her to take a one-month vacation so he could rent her shop to display his art. 3 This entrepreneurial spirit went in line with the transformative power which the period of Doi Moi promised. In opting against the traditional gallery space, Dinh was also able to access the general public – those who went to the mall to find themselves colorful, cute, and cheap products. Damaged Gene was just that – a children’s clothing kiosk with green wool sweaters decorated with flowers and small hearts, schoolgirl dresses laced with purple ribbons and bows. But immediately, one realizes that each sweater has two caps, each dress two collars, and each doll two heads.

In using the famous symbol of Siamese Twins to represent the effects of Agent Orange and merging it with baby clothing and toys, Dinh points out the socially constructed perceptions of purity and impurity, of acceptance and rejection. The open nature of the kiosk setting also allowed for genuine reactions of surprise, confusion, and intrigue. Having no way to justify why these clothing and toys felt so wrong, people could only ask what all of this was supposed to mean. As a result, Dinh was able to have many conversations with strangers, allowing for their interactions to serve as a replacement for the typical artist statement often seen in galleries or museums. As a temporary public art project, Damaged Gene welcomes unawareness and disorientation, creating a space for meaningful conversations on issues that often go un-discussed in society.

In parallel to challenging societal attitudes within his local Saigon community, Dinh became interested in exploring America’s post-war portrayal of the Vietnam war.

In the general view of the war, there are often two types of images. The first type is the documentary footage in the black and white films of Malcolm Browne, Nick Ut, and Eddie Addams. 4 The second type is everything that Hollywood made thereafter. Platoon , Deer Hunter , or Born on the Fourth of July — these are stories of self-affliction and discovery, of alcoholism and prostitution, exploring the wonders of Indochina and the almost-impossible return to America, and ever so often about the war itself. So even those who did not live through the war may feel that they have memories of it. But as more images are woven into people’s minds, it becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish fact from fiction.

In his 2000 series From Vietnam to Hollywood , Dinh employs the technique of weaving straw mats to reveal the fantasy world that has been imbued in our perceptions. In some of his large-scale photographic weavings, famous Hollywood film studios, such as Paramount, Columbia, and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, make up the background, while characters from both war movies and documentaries appear in the foreground, each seemingly ‘trapped’ in their own time and space. The contrasting images and explosion of interwoven colors make it difficult to distinguish which character comes from a movie and which comes from a documentary, who the bad guy and the good guy is. Within these dramatic scenes, Dinh discreetly integrates the third side of the story by including vernacular photographs of Vietnamese people of that time period. He weaves these characters as if they are in the process of disappearing from the image; the clarity with which they appear can therefore be viewed as the amount of ‘screen time’ they would get in history. As an attempt on Dinh’s part to reclaim his memory, the series in fact fully accepts reality’s defeat against Hollywood, where cinematic beauty and romantic despair will always be more interesting to believe in.

The inclusion of vernacular photographs seen in From Vietnam to Hollywood presents the question of how memories of others can be addressed in art. For Dinh, the answer came through collecting and living with these photographs over many years, until he could develop a form to adequately present them. Crossing the Farther Shore (2016) illustrates Vietnam’s Southern life from the 1940s to the 1980s — from weddings, beach trips, and family reunions, to newborn pictures and individual portraits. These snapshots depict moments of pure bliss, the sweet memories that people wanted to remember. The more images he found, the closer Dinh was brought to his own childhood memories. At the Songkhla refugee camp in Thailand where Dinh and his family stayed for a year in 1978, he remembers the clusters of mosquito nets that formed every night. Under the mosquito net, he could feel protected in the presence of his memories.

This structure also reminds Dinh of the Minimalism movement that was happening at around the same time. While people were protesting on the streets, the works of Donald Judd and Frank Stella seemed like a complete disregard for the war. But the anti-subjective, anti-traditional and symmetrical nature of the movement can also be understood as a silent protest that lays the foundation for starting anew. 5

These two parallel stories inspired Dinh to assemble 180 kilograms of found photographs into minimalist rectangular structures, made up of rows after rows of stringed images facing inwards and outwards, allowing the viewer from both sides to see the fronts as well as the backs containing real notes, excerpts from interviews, or passages from the Tale of Kieu by Nguyễn Du. 6 From the outside, the work is a tapestry of memory for people to learn from, image by image. 7 But on the inside, it becomes an intimate, safe, and collective place for the images to converse with each other. A delicate structure that holds the memories of a time of unprecedented conflict, Crossing the Farther Shore also carries the complex emotional weight of those who had to leave behind their belongings, photographs, and even close ones as they fled. Dinh has no way of knowing who each photograph belongs to, and he will most likely not find his own childhood pictures amongst the piles as he may have liked to, but he considers these lost images to be a sort of surrogate family to him. Thus, Crossing the Farther Shore , which was originally exhibited in Houston, becomes a way for Dinh to share the stories and histories of this extended ‘family’, not only with other Vietnamese Americans but also with the world.

Another crucial area of exploration for Dinh is his connection with both Vietnamese and Cambodian history. Dinh was born in 1968 in Ha Tien, a town next to the Cambodian border, which from 1967 to 1979 was caught in the middle of two conflicts. In 1977, The Khmer Rouge invaded his hometown, forcing his family to flee the country. So naturally, when Dinh returned to Vietnam in 1993, he also visited Cambodia. At the time, the only two sites for tourists to visit were Angkor Wat and Tuol Sleng, where the best and worst of humanity are exemplified in breathtaking capability. This immediately inspired Dinh’s series Cambodia: Splendor and Darkness which interlaces images of prisoners at Tuol Sleng with stylistic motifs of Angkor Wat.

Almost 30 years later, his series Monuments and Memorials still attempts to recreate Dinh’s feeling of visiting these two sites for the first time, but with a heightened focus on the role of architectural commemoration. His signature technique of interlacing vertical and horizontal strips merges the ‘bones’ – Tuol Sleng’s interior, with the ‘skin’ – Angkor Wat’s exterior, creating an optical illusion that brings to the front the meditative amber tone of both sites. 8 Depending on the eyes of the viewer, Tuol Sleng may be transformed into a beautifully decorated palace and Angkor Wat into an interior of consecutive broken doorways. There exists a balance of power in the constant silent battle between these sites. This effect is reflective of Dinh’s intention to speak about our tendency to build monuments over memorials. Monuments confer dominance over space and present “an aesthetic value as well as a political function.” 9 They are erected to celebrate a hero or an act of victory. But with every demonstration of victory, there is inevitable loss buried underneath. In the process of building over, alternative perspectives become inaccessible to our larger understanding of a time period overshadowed by biographies of greatness. This may just be the case of Angkor Wat’s dichotomy of victory and loss. In deconstructing and ‘de-monumentalizing’ the iconic monument of Angkor Wat, Dinh is viewing monuments as memorials of every country’s larger history.

Simultaneously embedded in his artistic journey are Dinh’s collaborative installations and video art projects. The Farmers and The Helicopters (2006) documents the process of a self-taught mechanic and a farmer making a helicopter, alongside a 3-channel video that discusses what this symbol of war means to them in the context of present-day Vietnam. 10 Here, art is not only physically made by others but also through the power of their own circumstance that builds relevance to the exploration. Another significant instance was Dinh’s decision to collaborate with Vietnamese war artists for the quinquennial documenta 13. 11 Seeing side by side a collection of their war sketches and a short documentary of the artists recounting their experiences, one can comprehend the emotional connection that these sketches are imbued with — hence giving a voice to both the soldiers and the artists. 12 Similar to Crossing the Farther Shore, here, Dinh is working with found objects that involve the stories and histories of others.

As explained by art critic Iwona Blazwick, “the found object is distinct from the ready-made in that it is for the most part unique.” 13 Dinh’s creation of art through these found objects is a way to give them a home. Because the particular stories he uncovers do not fit into normative history, he uses art’s ability to give objects a universal value, allowing them to be collectively preserved by art institutions. Here, they will be treated, displayed, shared, and studied about as archival records for the future, instead of sitting in Dinh’s personal collection and eventually returning back to the junk shops of Saigon. The project for documenta 13 indirectly addresses the research project of Vietnamese war photographers that led Dinh back to Vietnam 30 years prior. Thus, all of Dinh’s art projects can be seen as collaborations that have brought him closer to his initial goal, of finding and learning about the other side of history.

Dinh Q. Lê’s work reveals a trait inherent to his character – of working on the things that bother him until they feel resolved inside. This is why he has returned to many of his projects that have now become long-term. It began as a process of re-learning all that didn’t make him Vietnamese, which then became a never-ending journey of learning all that does make him Vietnamese. As he explained in an interview with curator Zoe Butt, “If you know history, you own it. An individual with no knowledge of his or her history is an individual without an identity.” 14 His journey of collecting, researching, interviewing, and taking photographs, is a way to live with history as it slowly unveils itself to him. Perhaps most significant, is how this learning process has allowed him to show that war is not the only thing inherent to Vietnamese culture. By exploring the layers of complexity and beauty in the stories of others, he sees the value of his own identity. As seen in his Cambodia projects, Dinh perhaps approaches his work best as a half-outsider stuck between the middle of two histories. So close yet so far away, it is exactly this in-betweenness that has given him the space to learn and adapt to the different circumstances life brings.

C 印刷和线条带. 从越南到好莱坞,2003年 艺术家的形象礼貌", "credit": "Matca", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在他的2000系列从越南到好莱坞中,Dinh采用了装饰品的技巧,以揭示了我们感知中沉浸的幻想世界。在他的一些大规模的摄影品中,著名的好莱坞电影工作室,如帕拉蒙特,哥伦比亚和Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer,形成了背景,而来自战争电影和纪录片的角色出现在前景中,每个人似乎在自己的时间和空间中“陷入困境”。很难区分哪个角色来自电影,哪个角色来自纪录片,谁是坏人和好人。在这些戏剧性的场景中,Dinh通过包括当时的越南人身影的故事的第三面,无情地整合了故事的第三面。他把这些角色看起来像他们正在从图像中消失的过程;他们出现的清晰度因此可以被视为他们在历史中获得的“屏幕时间”的数量。回归他的记忆,该系列实际上完全接受现实对好莱坞的失败,在那里电影的美丽和浪漫的绝望将永远更有趣地相信。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从越南到好莱坞看到的彩色照片的包含提出了如何在艺术中处理别人的记忆的问题。 对于迪恩,答案是通过收集和生活这些照片多年,直到他能够开发一种形式,以适当介绍它们。 跨越Farther Shore(2016)描绘了越南南生活从1940年代到1980年代 - 从婚礼,海滩旅行和家庭聚会,到新生儿的照片和个人肖像。人们想记住的甜蜜的记忆,他发现的更多图像,更接近的迪恩被带到他自己的童年记忆中,在泰国的Songkhla难民营,在那里迪恩和他的家人住了一年,1978年,他记得每晚形成的蚊子网的集群。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个结构也提醒了最小主义运动的宗教,发生在大约同一时间,人们在街道上抗议,唐纳德·朱德和弗兰克·斯特拉的作品似乎是对战争的完全忽视,但运动的反主观、反传统和同步性质也可以被理解为一个沉默的抗议,为重新开始奠定了基础。5", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/dinh_q_le_005-1024x687.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Matca", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/dinh_q_le_006-1024x680.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Dinh Q. article_text:
Daily Newsletter

The Art World Has an AI Problem

A diatribe against AI-generated art writing, MIT professors bedazzle security cameras, and Art Basel Paris goes into lockdown.

It’s not just a problem. It’s a travesty . AI in art writing, I mean — and if those words made you instinctively cringe, then you get it, because that “It’s not X, it’s Y” sentence construction is just one of the many hallmarks of artificially generated writing. Speaking as an editor, come on. We can tell. And we will judge, and let you know exactly how we feel about it. We might even write a diatribe against it, as Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia does today in a piece that is incisive, understanding, and original — a chatbot could never.

An opinion piece is one way to rail against the corporate-technological surveillance complex. Bedazzling security cameras is another, perhaps less orthodox, method. That’s right: Tenured professors at MIT are gluing googly eyes and rhinestones onto the university’s cameras, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports today, to protest its investment in Big Brother.

Sigh. To paraphrase Allen Ginsberg, I saw the best minds of my generation gluing craft materials onto surveillance apparatuses, and regurgitated as AI garbage.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia. | Valentina Di Liscia

title_original: Naïla Harzoune : « Plus qu’une écriture au féminin, c’est une écriture du trouble qui nous a toutes guidées. »
excerpt_original: Plongée tendue dans le quotidien moite de riches expatriés à Singapour, la série Singapura transforme le mystère à la White Lotus en une exploration du désir au féminin. La comédienne Naïla Harzoune nous emmène au cœur de cette série qui regarde les femmes autrement.
